A 10-day-old child presents with respiratory distress
and cyanosis. The CXR shows extensive bilateral
infiltrates and the SpO2 with O2 through non-
rebreather mask is around 80%. You decide to do a
hyperoxia test, where you measure the SpO2(PaO2)
before and after breathing 100% O2. What is NOT
true of hyperoxia test:
a. Rules out significant intra-cardiac and extra
cardiac (pulmonary) shunts
b. V/Q abnormalities may not show improvement
until 100% O2 is provided for the test
c. Failed test (no improvement in SpO2) in a
newborn confirms a congenital heart disease.
d. Intra-pulmonary shunts of > 50% are remarkably
resistant to 100% O2

a. O2 masks should never have flows less than 3-4

1. Which of the following statements is true about
blood pressure measurements in the PICU:
a. Oscillometric measurements are more
likely to overestimate the systolic and
underestimate the diastolic blood pressure.
b. Arterial pressure waveforms show

central to peripheral artery because of

c. Pressure wave travels about 10 times faster

d. The phenomenon of systolic amplification
is augmented in states of vasodilatory

Muscular Atrophy presents with altered sensorium
over last week. An arterial blood gas in room air
shows PaO2 40 mmHg, PaCO2 80 mmHg, and pH
of 7.29. Which of the following would explain her
hypoxemia?
a. Ventilation—perfusion mismatch
b. Intracardiac shunting
c. Intrapulmonary shunting
d. Alveolar hypoventilation

department 1 h after alleged ingestion of many
phenobarbitone tablets and is found to have SpO2-
82%. An ABG taken in room air shows PaO2 - 58,
PaCO2 -48, and pH -7.32. The patient is placed on a
100% face mask and some time later the SpO2 is
88%. Which of the following would explain her
hypoxemia?

4. A man has a pulmonary embolism that completely
blocks blood flow to his left lung. As a result, which
of the following will occur?
a. Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratio in the left
lung will be zero
b. Systemic arterial PO2 will be elevated
c. V/Q ratio in the left lung will be lower than
in the right lung
d. Alveolar PO2 in the left lung will be
approximately equal to the PO2 in inspired
air
e. Alveolar PO2 in the right lung will be
approximately equal to the PO2 in venous

5. A 12-year-old boy has a severe asthmatic attack
with wheezing. He worsens and becomes cyanotic.
His ABG PO2 - 60, and his PCO2 - 30.
Which of the following statements is most likely to
be true?
a. Forced expiratory volume/forced vital
capacity (FEV1/FVC) is increased
b. Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratio is
increased in the affected areas of his lungs
c. His arterial PCO2 is higher than normal
because of inadequate gas exchange
d. His arterial PCO2 is lower than normal
CRITICAL THINKING
causes of wide A-a gradient are shunts-
intrapulmonary or intracardiac and V/Q mismatch.
Failure of improvement of hypoxemia to 100%
oxygen makes V/Q mismatch unlikely. In an acute
setting with no prior history of cardiac disease,
intrapulmonary shunting (aspiration, pneumonia) is
the most likely.
4. Answer: d
Explanation: The V/Q in left lung with no perfusion
would be ∞, with lowering of PO2. Alveolar PO2
would equilibrate with alveolar PO2 without any
improvement in systemic PO2 because of absence of
any perfusion.
5. Answer: d
Explanation: Hypoxia induces a strong respiratory
drive mediated by the carotid and aortic body
chemoreceptors. This induces respiratory alkalosis
untill the drive is able to compensate.
6. Answer: b
Explanation: Elastance is the reciprocal of
compliance. Compliance can be calculated from the
given data, C= dV/ dP, 100/20=5 ml/cmH20. The
elastance of the respiratory system is 1/C= 0.2
cmH20/ml.
7. Answer: c
Explanation: The child is hemodynamically stable
without any active bleed in the PICU. Platelet
counts and coagulation profile are reasonable for a
child with no active bleed. Hypothermia along with
acidosis and tissue hypoperfusion can worsen
PICU Quiz
coagulopathy in a post-traumatic bleeding child.
Hypothermia should be corrected now.
8. Answer: d
Explanation: The situation of withdrawal after
prolonged opioid and/or benzodiazepine use in
ICUs is neither unknown nor uncommon. There are
many ways of dealing with withdrawal mostly
including restarting of opioid with very gradual
tapering. Clonidine with its central alpha2 agonist
activity is often added to this regime. Oral morphine
when started needs to be about 4-5 times the
intravenous dose. Switching from Morphine to
Fentanyl offers no advantage. Amongst the options
provided “d” is the most logical.
9. Answer: b
Explanation: The graphic is representative of APRV,
Airway Pressure Release Ventilation. This is an
extreme form of inverse ratio ventilation and allows
patient to breathe spontaneously while delivering
mandated “release” breaths. The release is kept
short, a low Tlow. The Plow can be set at zero
ensuring the flow doesnot go down to zero, by using
a shorter Tlow. Patients can contribute upto 40% of
MV.
10. Answer: d
Explanation: The graph is of PaO2 vs CaO2 the
oxygen content (1.34 x Hb x Sa02 + 0.003 x Pa02).
A drop on content from A to B can be easily
explained by a drop in hemoglobin, bleeding.

1. A 9-month-old boy presents with difficulty
breathing. His mother states that he has been
treated for croup twice already in the last 4
months with similar symptoms. He has had 2 days
of upper respiratory tract infection symptoms and
now has expiratory stridor on examination. Which
of the following is correct?
a. Recurrent acute laryngotracheobronchitis
(croup) needs further investigation and should
not be ignored
b. Intrathoracic airway obstruction is typically
worse during inspiration
c. Extrathoracic airway obstruction is typically
worse during inspiration
d. Croup (viral laryngotracheobronchitis) is
typically characterized by intrathoracic airway
obstruction
e. All are true
2. A patient with acute respiratory distress syndrome
has been managed with high-frequency oscillatory
ventilation for the past 2 hours. A blood gas study
shows pH of 7.48, PaCO2 of 30 mm Hg, PaO2
of 70 mm Hg, bicarbonate level of 22 mEq/L.
and oxygen saturation of 97% on a FIO2 of 0.6.
Which of the following is the most appropriate
intervention?
a. Wean the mean airway pressure.
b. Increase the delta P.
c. Decrease the frequency.
d. Increase the mean airway pressure.
e. Increase the frequency.

bronchiolitis. You extubate him today and almost
immediately notice a significant stridor. Which of
the following is true of this condition?
a. Occurs in 50% of children.
b. Begins within 18 hours, peaks at 48 hours,
and resolves by 5 days.
c. Patients with active coughing and very light
sedation are less likely to develop this
[hinking

c Intensivist Pulmonologist
ital. New Delhi
g-2014 /Published online:15-Aug-2014
d. More prevalent in children above 5 years of
age who have undergone neck surgery.
e. All of the above.
4. A 12 year 48 kg boy with deep burns to about
85% body surface area involving most of trunk
and lower extremities is admitted to your ICU,
intubated and ventilated. His ventilatory parameters
are: Synchronized intermittent mandatory
ventilation+Pressure  Control/Pressure Support,
rate 25, pressures (Peak inspiratory pressure over
PEEP/PEEP) 32+6/6, (Tidal volume generated
160ml) Inspiratory time 0.9 sec, FiO2 1. ABG
shows pH 7.2, pCO2 82, pO2 52, HCO3 18.
Chest Radiograph: clear fields.
What is the most appropriate measure?
a. Acceptable parameters, continue on same
settings avoiding further injury to lungs
b. Escharotomy of chest wound
c. Increase PEEP. likely developing ALI (Acute
lung injury)
d. Switch to High Frequency Oscillatory
Ventilation (HFOV). needs higher Mean
Airway Pressure
e. Bronchoscopic toilet of lungs
5. A 15-day-old child is brought in respiratory
distress. A Chest radiograph done shows
markedly increased pulmonary vascularity.
The echocardiogram shows Double Inlet
Right Ventricle(DIRV) and confirms torrential
pulmonary flows. The vitals: HR 178, BP 50/28,
RR 90, SPO2-98%.ABG: pH 7.25, pCO2 35, pO2
90, BE -13. lactate 6.
The child is intubated and initiated on mechanical
ventilation. The cardiologist and surgeons plan
for pulmonary artery banding which can only
happen the next morning. Over the next few hours
the child has drop in urine output and the ABG on
room air shows- pH 7.20, pCO2 40, pO2 84. BE
-17, lactate 9.
CRITICAL THINKING
2. Answer: e
A child with ARDS is hyperventilated on the
HFOV as suggested by the pH and the PaCO2
levels. The SpO2 is reasonable on 60% FiO2
and attempts to wean mean airway pressure
would be a little premature. Ventilation (CO2
washout) is a function of tidal volume (read
delta P) and frequency on the HFOV. Increasing
delta P would washout CO2 even further by
increasing the swing of the piston and the tidal
volume. Contrary to conventional ventilation,
frequency has an inverse relationship to CO2 and
increasing the frequency (hertz) would increase
the PaCO2.
3. Answer: e
This is the condition of postextubation croup.
It occurs in approximately 5% of intubated
children and usually resolves in 24 hours. It is
more common in patients with frequent coughing
episodes and in patients who are more agitated
and moving frequently while intubated. It has
been shown to be more prevalent in children 1-4
years or age, particularly in association with any
type of surgery in the head/neck area.
4. Answer: b
The scenario is of extrinsic restriction of lung
expansion most likely due to eschar formations on
trunk. Escharotomy of all circumferential burns
should be undertaken as an emergency. Some
incomplete eschars may need excision too to help
chest expansion.
5. Answer: b
This is a situation of single ventricle physiology.
Unrestricted pulmonary blood flows is causing
systemic hypoperfusion and shock.Pulmonary
artery(PA) banding is the emergency procedure
of choice but in a situation that it cannot be
performed immediately inhaled nitrogen or
carbon dioxide can be used to induce hypoxemic
pulmonary vasoconstriction to improve systemic
blood flow.
Conflict of Interest: None Source of Funding: None
PICU Quiz
6. Answer: e
Subglottic stenosis is an uncommon complication
of tracheal intubation. A larger than adequate
tube is the most common association but sepsis,
GER and eosinophilic esophagitis have all been
implicated in the formation of subglottic stenosis.
7. Answer: a
Lung infection and positive pressure ventilation
both cause an inappropriate increase of ADH and
cause the body to hold on to free water: Extubation
would reverse this and cause spontaneous diuresis.
For a child who has improved, use of Frusemide
or Dopamine cannot be justified.
8. Answer: c
The child has fulminant hepatic failure. Control
of airways in a comatose child, hemodynamic
support, prophylactic antibiotics and antiedema
measures are all accepted treatment modalities
for the child. Lactulose is not preferred because of
the risks of aspiration, ileus and lack of outcome
benefits and is no longer recommended.
9. Answer: d
The Cochrane metanalysis and review on this
topic (Khemani RG, Randolph A, Markovitz B.
Corticosteroids for the prevention and treatment of
post-extubation stridor in neonates, children and
adults. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
2009) shows that steroids may be of benefit in
infants and children with airway abnormalities in
reducing post extubation stridor. Steroids begun
pre-extubation in adults does reduce the incidence
of stridor but not of reintubation.
10. Answer: d
An adequate ratio of nitrogenous to total
calories is justified to ensure proper utilization
of exogenous proteins. The desired ratio of N:
NonNitrogen calorie of 1: 250-350 is generally
recommended. This is the same as having a
protein: non-protein calorie ratio of 1: 25-35.
This calorie concentration can be safely given
through the central line.

8. Answer A
Rationale:
Appropriate antibiotic coverage is critical to
successful treatment of acute bacterial meningitis.
Gram-negative meningitis may require an antibiotic
course as long as 3 weeks. Antibiotic resistance has
become a real issue in both community and hospital
clinical settings. The Klebsiella strain described in
this scenario is noted to be extended-spectrum beta-
lactamase positive. Although its antibiogram shows
sensitivity to beta-lactam antibiotics, it is at high risk
for becoming a resistant strain. Aminoglycosides are
not affected by beta-lactamases. Clindamycin is not
appropriate for gram-negative infections.

notes: Many algorithms give dantrolene as soon as possible alongside hyperventilation with 100% O2; the quiz key places O2 washout first.
This quiz's printed key gave 'excessive sensitivity to PTH'. The same question appears in Quiz 22 of this file, keyed to the parathyroid answer, which matches the physiology and is shown here.
10207.explanation: Raised calcium should suppress PTH via the calcium-sensing receptor. A 'normal' PTH in hypercalcaemia is inappropriately high, so the problem is parathyroid autonomy (primary hyperparathyroidism).

notes: Options for Q3, Q4 and Q6 were misprinted in the original layout; they are re-assigned here to match the answer key.
Later trials (ProCESS, ARISE, ProMISe) found no mortality benefit from protocolised EGDT; ScvO2 remains one of several resuscitation markers.
Hypercalcaemia also increases digoxin toxicity, but hypokalaemia is the classic keyed answer.
The printed key says 'E', but its own rationale states DTRs are compatible with brain death and posturing is not — the answer shown follows the rationale (B).
Many classifications (e.g., PALICC/Berlin) list near-drowning as a direct insult; the answer follows the source key.
The stem is incomplete in the original; the bracketed wording reflects the answer rationale.
Later studies show pulse oximetry can overestimate SaO2 in darker skin; the keyed answer (jaundice) remains correct.
The printed key reads 'A', but its rationale describes ciclosporin (option B).
qSOFA was derived in adults; it is not validated for paediatric sepsis (Phoenix criteria, 2024).

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
11903.explanation: Neurological injury patterns (haemorrhage, infarction, seizures, developmental delay) are broadly similar in cardiac and respiratory ECMO survivors.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary. Adult respiratory ECMO has grown substantially since this quiz (2017).
11904.explanation: Cardiac failure needs VA support; neonatal respiratory ECMO has declined (surfactant, iNO, HFOV); E-CPR is established. Answer as keyed: none of the statements.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
11905.explanation: Answer as keyed: renal failure alters heparin clearance, so requirements change when CRRT is added; monitor anticoagulation closely.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
11906.explanation: Cardiac arrest needs circulatory as well as respiratory support → veno-arterial ECMO.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
11907.explanation: E-CPR is reasonable for in-hospital arrest when the cause is reversible (or bridge to transplant), CPR is high quality with minimal no-flow, and the team can cannulate rapidly — typically in cardiac patients in settings with ECMO protocols.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
11908.explanation: A non-ejecting LV on VA ECMO distends and raises LA pressure; decompress the left heart with an LA vent or balloon/blade atrial septostomy.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
11909.explanation: Anticoagulated ECMO patients risk major bleeding from chest drains; small, haemodynamically insignificant pneumothoraces are observed while the lungs rest.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary. Some studies (e.g., Rich et al., 1998) found femoro-atrial flow (drain IVC, return to RA) gave less recirculation; check local practice.
The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
11911.explanation: On VV ECMO, oxygenated return mixes with native venous blood, so SaO2 of ~80–85% is acceptable if Hb and cardiac output keep oxygen delivery adequate.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
11912.explanation: Blood leaving the lungs (arterial) has the same saturation as blood entering them (PA): the native lungs add no oxygen; all oxygenation comes from the circuit.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
11913.explanation: Bleeding is managed by raising platelet/fibrinogen targets, antifibrinolytics and surgical exploration while continuing (perhaps reduced) anticoagulation; stopping heparin risks circuit thrombosis.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
11914.explanation: Oxygenation depends mainly on ECMO blood flow (fraction of cardiac output passing the oxygenator); CO2 removal depends on sweep gas flow.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
11915.explanation: SvO2 ~70–75% indicates adequate oxygen delivery relative to consumption during the trial off.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
11916.explanation: Platelets adhere to and are activated by the circuit surface and are consumed continuously; platelet transfusion is the most frequent product given.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
11917.explanation: Intracranial haemorrhage is the most consequential bleeding complication (major cause of death and disability), particularly in neonates.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
11918.explanation: Heparin binds antithrombin, accelerating its inactivation of thrombin and factor Xa ~1000-fold; low antithrombin causes heparin resistance.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
11919.explanation: On VA ECMO the pre-membrane (venous drainage) saturation reflects mixed venous O2 and therefore the balance of delivery and consumption.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
11920.explanation: Recirculation (reinfused oxygenated blood drained straight back) rises with high pump flow, cannula tips positioned close together, small RA size, and low cardiac output.

notes: Option D is also factually true (M protein is a GAS virulence factor); the keyed best answer is A.
In practice, IV acyclovir should be started immediately in an immunocompromised child with varicella pneumonitis alongside PCR confirmation.

12201.explanation: PTH inhibits proximal-tubular phosphate reabsorption (phosphaturia), increases distal calcium reabsorption, stimulates 1α-hydroxylation of vitamin D and mobilises bone calcium — it raises, not lowers, serum calcium.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12202.explanation: Aldosterone increases ENaC-mediated sodium reabsorption and K+/H+ secretion in the collecting duct → sodium retention, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary. Current evidence emphasises the podocyte slit diaphragm (nephrin) as a key size barrier.
12203.explanation: Answer as keyed: negatively charged heparan-sulphate proteoglycans of the GBM provide a charge barrier repelling anionic albumin.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12204.explanation: Repolarisation occurs when outward K+ current exceeds inward current. Hyperkalaemia depolarises (less negative) the membrane; cardioplegia uses HIGH K+ to arrest the heart; the upstroke is via voltage-gated Na+ channels, not the pump.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12205.explanation: Iodotyrosine deiodinase (dehalogenase) in the thyrocyte recycles iodide from mono- and diiodotyrosine. T4 is the predominant product; iodination/coupling occurs on thyroglobulin at the apical (luminal) surface; proteolysis occurs in thyrocyte lysosomes after endocytosis.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12206.explanation: Glucagon acts via a G-protein-coupled receptor (cAMP) in the liver to rapidly increase glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; it stimulates lipolysis. GLUT4 is insulin-dependent (muscle/fat), not brain.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12207.explanation: Hypercalcaemia should suppress PTH; a normal (high-normal) PTH is inappropriate and indicates primary hyperparathyroidism.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary. CCK can modestly inhibit acid via somatostatin; the keyed answer treats it as non-regulatory.
12208.explanation: Answer as keyed: acid secretion is stimulated by acetylcholine (vagus), gastrin and histamine (H2).

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12209.explanation: NO inhibits smooth-muscle proliferation and platelet aggregation; endothelin is a vasoconstrictor and mitogen with positive inotropic effects.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12210.explanation: Poiseuille's law: flow ∝ r⁴, so halving the radius reduces flow to (1/2)⁴ = 1/16 (resistance rises 16-fold).

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12301.explanation: Atracurium/cisatracurium degrade spontaneously (Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis) independent of liver and kidney. Vecuronium and pancuronium have active metabolites that accumulate in renal/hepatic failure; rocuronium depends on hepatic/renal clearance.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12302.explanation: JET is an automatic tachycardia, so cardioversion is ineffective. Management: reduce catecholamines, sedation, cooling (34–35 °C), correct electrolytes (Mg), atrial pacing above the JET rate, amiodarone.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12303.explanation: After successful repair a large residual arm–leg gradient (40 mmHg) is uncommon. Recognised complications: paradoxical (rebound) hypertension, mesenteric arteritis (post-coarctectomy syndrome), spinal cord ischaemia, and associated berry aneurysm rupture.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary. Current evidence suggests ketamine does not raise ICP in ventilated patients and preserves BP; many now favour it or etomidate in haemodynamically unstable TBI.
12304.explanation: Answer as keyed: propofol reduces CMRO2 and ICP and gives smooth induction, but it can cause hypotension, which must be avoided in TBI.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12305.explanation: With prolonged exposure (>5–7 days), methadone weaning should begin pre-emptively as infusions are tapered, not after withdrawal appears; monitor with a withdrawal score (e.g., WAT-1).

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary. Cannon a waves classically indicate AV dissociation (e.g., JET, complete heart block) — the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve; TR produces large v waves.
12306.explanation: Answer as keyed (Ebstein anomaly — large a waves from atrial contraction against a poorly compliant atrialised RV/abnormal tricuspid valve).

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12307.explanation: On HFOV, CO2 clearance ∝ f × VT²; raising frequency shortens each cycle and reduces delivered VT, so ventilation worsens. A cuff leak, higher ΔP or longer IT increase CO2 removal.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12308.explanation: Heliox is not a bronchodilator and has no anti-inflammatory effect; it only lowers gas density to reduce turbulent flow and work of breathing while definitive therapy works.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12309.explanation: Hypothermia is a confounder: core temperature must be normalised (>35 °C) before brain-death examination. 'Doll's eye positive' (eyes fixed in the orbit as the head turns) actually means absent oculocephalic reflex; spinal reflexes (e.g., Lazarus-type arm movements) can occur; ancillary tests are not mandatory.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12310.explanation: Hyponatraemia + high urine output + hypovolaemia (low CVP, poor perfusion) after brain injury = cerebral salt wasting. SIADH is euvolaemic with low urine output; DI causes hypernatraemia.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12401.explanation: PaO2 50 → SaO2 ~85%; PaO2 100 → ~98%. CaO2 = 1.34 × 10 × SaO2 + 0.003 × PaO2 rises from ≈11.5 to ≈13.4 mL/dL (≈15%) — more than 10% because saturation rises on the steep part of the curve.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12402.explanation: ~70–90% of CO2 is carried as bicarbonate (via carbonic anhydrase), ~5–10% dissolved and ~5–10% as carbamino compounds.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12403.explanation: TRALI: acute hypoxaemia with BILATERAL infiltrates within 6 h of transfusion, non-cardiogenic (often donor anti-HLA/HNA antibodies) — fluid overload is TACO.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12404.explanation: PTLD is mostly B-cell, EBV-driven; risk factors include EBV-seronegative recipient of a seropositive organ, young age and intense T-cell immunosuppression. Lymphadenopathy, tonsillar enlargement, fever and GI symptoms are common.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12405.explanation: Low rate, long expiratory time and permissive hypercapnia limit dynamic hyperinflation, barotrauma and haemodynamic compromise; avoid prolonged paralysis (myopathy with steroids).

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12406.explanation: ARDS is fundamentally increased permeability of the alveolar–capillary membrane, causing protein-rich oedema; atelectasis, surfactant dysfunction and V/Q mismatch follow.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12407.explanation: Hypoventilation (and low inspired PO2) lowers PAO2 and PaO2 equally, so the A–a gradient stays normal. Diffusion limit, V/Q mismatch and shunt all widen it.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12408.explanation: CO binds Hb ~240× more avidly than O2; pulse oximetry and calculated SaO2 read falsely normal while O2 content and delivery fall → lactic acidosis. Measure COHb by co-oximetry; consider cyanide co-poisoning.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12409.explanation: MAP = [(Ti × PIP) + (Te × PEEP)] / (Ti + Te). Expiration occupies most of the cycle, so raising PEEP raises MAP the most (and PIP also rises in PRVC).

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12410.explanation: At lower frequency each oscillation lasts longer, so delivered VT increases; since HFOV CO2 clearance ∝ f × VT², the gain in VT outweighs the fall in frequency.

notes: Option B is also true per the same rationale; the keyed best answer is E.
The source also says haemofiltration prolongs the half-life (option B); age dependence is the keyed answer.
The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12701.explanation: AECC (1994): acute onset, bilateral infiltrates, no left-atrial hypertension; PaO2/FiO2 ≤300 = ALI, ≤200 = ARDS. Here 92/0.45 ≈ 204 → ALI. ('Mild/moderate/severe' are Berlin 2012 categories.)

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12702.explanation: Shunted blood never contacts alveolar gas, so raising FiO2 adds little (especially with large shunts). All other mechanisms improve with supplemental oxygen.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12703.explanation: Paediatric trials of tight glycaemic control (e.g., after cardiac surgery) consistently increased hypoglycaemia without clear benefit in infection or outcome.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12704.explanation: Initial severe-TBI care: secure airway, normocapnia, avoid hypotension/hypoxia, ICP monitoring/CSF drainage, hyperosmolar therapy. Decompressive craniectomy is reserved for refractory intracranial hypertension.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12705.explanation: Outcome after diffuse TBI is driven largely by primary neuronal/axonal injury; controlling ICP prevents secondary injury but cannot reverse the primary lesion (DECRA trial context).

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12706.explanation: Answer as keyed: in paediatric in-hospital arrest studies, needing ≥4 epinephrine doses (reflecting prolonged CPR) was associated with poor functional outcome in nearly all survivors.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12707.explanation: 2011 guidelines: brain death is a clinical diagnosis — two examinations, each with an apnoea test; ancillary tests are not required; spinal reflexes (e.g., DTRs) are compatible; guidelines do not apply to infants <37 weeks.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12708.explanation: 2011 SCCM/AAP/CNS guideline: 24 h for term neonates (37 wk to 30 days) and 12 h for infants and children >30 days to 18 years.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12709.explanation: Sepsis is the factor most strongly associated with mortality in ventilated children with leukaemia (same item as Quiz 9).

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12710.explanation: Outcomes for children with low-risk ALL — even after PICU support with organ failure — are good, so full support including RRT is appropriate.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12711.explanation: Over time ECMO was increasingly offered to children with comorbidities (e.g., immunodeficiency, malignancy, chronic disease), who have lower survival — offsetting technical improvements.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12712.explanation: Answer as keyed: tidal volume (alveolar overdistension/volutrauma) was most significantly associated with pneumothorax.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12713.explanation: Hyperoxic resuscitation generates free radicals and has been linked to cerebral injury and higher mortality; guidelines start term neonates on room air (21%) and titrate.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12714.explanation: Injury severity is a major confounder: sicker brains have both more seizures and worse outcomes, so association does not prove causation.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12801.explanation: Most acid is excreted as NH4+ (ammoniagenesis rises markedly in acidosis); titratable acid (phosphate) is limited and free H+ is trivial (urine pH ≥4.5). Hyperventilation is respiratory compensation, not renal elimination.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12802.explanation: Apical NHE3 secretes most H+; basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase creates the gradient; bicarbonate reclamation needs carbonic anhydrase; proximal luminal pH falls only to ~6.7 (distal can reach ~4.5).

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12803.explanation: CO2 crosses the blood–brain barrier freely, but CSF has little protein and haemoglobin buffering, so CSF pH falls faster than blood pH. Renal compensation takes days.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12804.explanation: ANP (released with atrial stretch) increases GFR and inhibits sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct, and suppresses renin and aldosterone → natriuresis and diuresis.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12805.explanation: Volume expansion raises preload, cardiac output, renal blood flow and GFR, stretches the atria (↑ANP) and suppresses renin.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary. Statement A is generally true (PGE2/PGI2, dopamine via D1 and bradykinin are vasodilators), so this key appears flawed.
The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12807.explanation: Angiotensin II stimulates proximal NHE3 sodium reabsorption, causes arteriolar vasoconstriction and stimulates aldosterone release.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12808.explanation: Proximal water reabsorption (~65% of filtrate) is iso-osmotic, following solute (largely Na+ via NHE3) through abundant AQP1 channels, aided by peritubular oncotic pressure.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12809.explanation: Depolarisation = potential becomes less negative/more positive; more negative = hyperpolarisation. Resting potential is negative inside, measured between an inside and an outside electrode.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12810.explanation: VT is a fast ventricular rhythm; short diastole impairs filling, so output and BP can fall dangerously. It is not a bradycardia.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12811.explanation: Systolic pressure rises with stiffer vessels and larger or faster ejection; slower ejection lowers systolic pressure.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12812.explanation: Inotropes INCREASE dP/dt max, velocity of shortening, ejection rate and stroke volume.

notes: The source gives the answer key only; the explanation is a brief standard summary.
12813.explanation: Answer as keyed: end-systolic volume is set by contractility and afterload (the ESPVR), largely independent of preload; preload changes EDV, SV, EF and CO (Frank–Starling).

notes: Option A is also good practice (recurrent/atypical croup warrants airway evaluation), but the keyed answer is C.
The printed key is 'E', but the source's own rationale contradicts every statement — treat this item as flawed.
A later Cochrane update suggests steroids may also reduce reintubation in high-risk adults.
Cross-reactivity between sulfonamide antibiotics and non-antibiotic sulfonamides such as furosemide is now considered uncommon.
Current practice for ESBL meningitis is a carbapenem (e.g., meropenem); aminoglycosides penetrate CSF poorly as monotherapy.

10908.explanation: Answer as keyed: the presence of sepsis is associated with the worst survival (no further rationale given in the source).

10105.explanation: Neck flexion moves the ETT tip down toward the carina ("the hose follows the nose"); extension moves it up.

10208.explanation: With a fixed Ti, the cycle time (60/rate) shortens as rate increases, so all the shortening falls on expiratory time. With an I:E ratio, Ti changes with rate; an inspiratory hold may delay expiration; normal Ti is far shorter than 3–4 s.

10209.explanation: All raise pulmonary vascular resistance/RV afterload: PE (mechanical obstruction), protamine (acute pulmonary vasoconstriction), ARDS (hypoxic vasoconstriction, high PEEP), OSA (chronic hypoxic pulmonary hypertension).

10210.explanation: Proning makes ventilation distribution more homogeneous via changes in chest-wall/abdominal compliance and lung shape matching. PROSEVA showed a mortality benefit; proning aids secretion drainage; sessions of ~16 h were used.
